overview.intro: Why did States come into existence at all? This unit examines the answers political thought has given. The divine origin theory holds that authority descends from God; the social contract theories of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau hold that human beings created the State by agreement to escape a condition they found intolerable or insecure. Comparing them shows how differently the same institution can be justified, and what each justification implies about the rights of the governed.

learningOutcomes: Explain the divine origin theory and its features.
Describe the state of nature in each social contract theory.

blocks.text: The oldest justification of political authority is that it comes from God. In this account the king holds his crown as a divine deposit, his person is sacred because his office is sacred, and resistance to his command is therefore resistance to the divine order itself. James I of England argued the case in writing against the claims of Parliament, and the doctrine appeared in different forms across cultures, from the anointing of European monarchs to the conception of divine kingship elsewhere. Its political function was straightforward: it placed the ruler’s authority beyond the reach of argument, since a claim grounded in revelation cannot be refuted by evidence.

The theory has four features usually examined together. Authority descends from above rather than arising from below; it is hereditary in its transmission; it is absolute, since no human institution can review a divine appointment; and it is therefore beyond question, which is both its strength as a stabilising idea and its weakness as a political argument. As an explanation of how States actually began it explains nothing, since States existed before the particular theology that justified them, and as a justification it proves too much, because rival dynasties could each claim the same blessing. Its historical importance lies in the resistance it provoked: if authority came from God to the ruler, later thinkers asked, then to whom did the rights of the people come?

learn.title: The social contract: Hobbes and Locke

blocks.text: Social contract theories share a method rather than a conclusion: they imagine human beings before government, describe the condition they would be in, and then explain the State as the product of their choice. For Hobbes, writing in the English civil war, the state of nature was a condition of perfect freedom but also of perpetual fear, in which every person had a right to everything including the body of another, and life was solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. Reason suggested peace, so individuals covenant with one another to transfer all their rights to a sovereign — the Leviathan — who cannot be punished because the covenant was made with each other and not with him. The result is absolute authority: the sovereign makes the laws, defines property and cannot be resisted, because to permit resistance is to reopen the war everyone escaped.

Locke rejected that conclusion. For him the state of nature was governed by natural law, which gave every person rights to life, liberty and property, but its defect was that there was no impartial judge to settle disputes. People therefore contract not to surrender their rights but to create a government that will protect them, and they retain the power to dissolve that government when it acts against its trust. Government is thus fiduciary: the sovereign is the legislature, it rules by established laws, and taxation requires consent because property is what the government exists to secure. The difference matters politically — Hobbes justifies obedience, Locke justifies revolution — and the difference arises entirely from a different description of the condition that preceded the State.

blocks.text: Rousseau’s contract differs from both. He begins by attacking the alternatives: property, inequality and the convention that made the first occupier a proprietor, all of which he traces to a historical act of appropriation rather than to nature. His solution is that each person puts himself and his powers in common under the direction of the general will, and in so doing remains as free as before, because obedience to a law that he prescribes to himself as a member of the sovereign is not loss of freedom but its exercise. The sovereign cannot legislate for particular individuals, the general will always aims at the common good even when the people are mistaken about what it is, and the government is merely an agent of the sovereign and can be changed at will.

Rousseau also supplies the answer to the standing objection that no one ever signed such an agreement. The contract is not a historical event but a legitimate order: if a person refused the civil order, society could compel him to obey, and in being compelled he would in effect be forced to be free, since the obligation he owes to himself as a citizen is the same as the obligation he owes to his own reason. Critics have found that formula troubling precisely because it shows how a theory of freedom can justify coercion, and the tension between the general will and the wishes of actual majorities remains one of the most discussed problems in democratic theory.

items: All three contract theories justify the State by appeal to the people rather than to God.
Hobbes grounds them in fear, Locke in rights and consent, Rousseau in collective self-legislation.
Each theory’s conclusion follows from its description of the pre-political condition.
Rousseau’s general will is not the will of all: it aims at the common good.
The contract is best read as a standard of legitimacy, not as an event in history.

learn.title: Assessment: what the contract theories explain and what they do not

blocks.text: The strength of the contract method is that it relocates authority in the people. Once legitimacy is a matter of agreement or trust, the ruler becomes answerable, property and rights become claims against government, and resistance becomes a political rather than a sacrilegious question. That is why both the English settlement of 1688 and the American declaration of independence spoke the language of contract, and why the ideas travel so easily into constitutional drafting.

The weaknesses are well rehearsed. No historical compact can be produced, so the theory must be read as fiction or as a standard of legitimacy; people are born into states they never joined; and the reasoning is circular in places, since Hobbes derives obligation from a promise made where no obligation yet existed. Yet the objection that the contract never happened misses its use: the theory answers the question of what would make authority legitimate, and by that test many governments plainly fail. A strong answer therefore distinguishes explanation from justification — contract theories explain poorly how States began but justify powerfully what makes rule legitimate — and then judges each thinker by the internal consistency of his own account.

keyPoints: The divine origin theory holds that kings rule by God’s appointment and resistance is sacrilege.

questions.prompt: The phrase solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short describes:
questions.explanation: Hobbes used the phrase to describe life without a common power to keep everyone in awe.

questions.prompt: Which thinker held that the people may dissolve a government that breaks its trust?
questions.explanation: For Locke government is fiduciary: it exists to protect natural rights and may be dissolved when it fails in that trust.

questions.prompt: The divine origin theory implies that resistance to the king is:
questions.explanation: If the crown is God’s appointment, resistance is resistance to the divine order itself.

questions.prompt: Rousseau’s claim that a person forced to obey the law would in effect be forced to be free rests on the idea that:
options: The citizen is a member of the sovereign and obeys a law prescribed to himself
The general will is the sum of private desires
questions.answer: The citizen is a member of the sovereign and obeys a law prescribed to himself
questions.explanation: Obligation to the collective self-legislation is obligation to one’s own reason, so obedience is not subjection; the general will aims at the common good and is not a tally of private wants.

questions.prompt: The book in which Hobbes set out his absolute sovereign is the __________ .
questions.explanation: Published in 1651, it argued that only undivided authority could end the state of nature.

questions.prompt: For Rousseau, the will that always aims at the common good is the general __________ .
questions.explanation: It differs from the will of all, which is the sum of private interests.

questions.prompt: State four features of the divine origin theory.
questions.answer: Four features are: authority descends from God rather than arising from the people; the office is transmitted by hereditary succession rather than by merit or election; the authority of the ruler is absolute, since no human institution may review a divine appointment; and the claim is beyond question, so resistance counts as sacrilege rather than as politics. The sacred character of the ruler’s person follows from the sanctity of the office and is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each feature must be stated with its implication, not merely listed.

questions.prompt: How does Hobbes’ state of nature differ from Locke’s?
questions.answer: Hobbes’ state of nature is a condition of perfect formal equality in which every person has a right to everything, including the body of another, so that competition, diffidence and glory produce a perpetual war of all against all and life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. Locke’s state of nature, by contrast, is governed by natural law discerned by reason, which gives everyone rights to life, liberty and property and imposes a duty not to harm another in those respects. The defect of Hobbes’ condition is the absence of a common power to keep everyone in awe; the defect of Locke’s is the absence of an impartial judge and a known law to settle disputes. The difference explains their conclusions: Hobbes transfers all rights to an absolute sovereign, while Locke creates a government to protect rights that are retained, with a right to dissolve it when it breaks trust.
questions.explanation: Three paired contrasts are required, each tied to the different conclusion about sovereignty.

questions.prompt: Compare the social contract theories of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau.
questions.answer: All three replace divine sanction with a human act: they describe a condition before government and derive the State from the choice made in it, but each description yields a different polity. Hobbes begins with a war of all against all produced by equality, scarcity and the absence of a common power; reason counsels peace, so individuals covenant to transfer every right to a sovereign who cannot be punished, since the covenant ran between them and not with him. The result is absolute and indivisible authority: the Leviathan makes the laws, defines property and cannot be resisted, because any permitted resistance reopens the war. Locke begins with natural law but no impartial judge; people therefore contract to appoint a government whose task is to protect life, liberty and property, they surrender only the private enforcement of natural law, and they retain the power to dissolve a government that acts against its trust. Rousseau begins with appropriation and inequality, and his contract unites each person with all others under the general will, so that the citizen remains as free as before because obedience to a law he prescribes to himself is the exercise of freedom rather than its loss; the sovereign is the citizen body itself, and government is its replaceable agent. The comparison shows that the state of nature does the argumentative work: fear in Hobbes, the wish for a judge in Locke, and the corruption produced by property in Rousseau. Judged internally, Hobbes is the most consistent and the least liberal, Locke the most usable in constitutional practice, and Rousseau the most demanding, since he requires citizens capable of subordinating private interest to the common good.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all three theories with their state of nature, contract and conclusion compared on the same bases, plus a judgement.

questions.prompt: Social contract theories explain poorly how States began but justify powerfully what makes rule legitimate. Discuss.
questions.answer: As explanations of origins the theories are weak in ways their own authors partly conceded. Archaeology and anthropology show no single transition from a state of nature to civil society: institutions grew over generations through settlement, agriculture, kinship and conquest, and there is no moment at which dispersed individuals assembled to sign. Hobbes’ derivation of obligation from a promise is circular, since the covenant he describes presupposes the moral duty it is meant to create, and Locke’s argument that people tacitly consent by remaining in a territory stretches consent until it can be extracted from anyone who merely passes through. Judged as history, therefore, the theories are fictions. As standards of legitimacy they are far stronger, because each isolates a condition under which rule would be rightful and then tests actual governments against it. On Locke’s test a government that legislates without consent, that taxes arbitrarily or that attacks property fails the test regardless of its antiquity, which is precisely why the language of contract furnished arguments for the English revolution of 1688 and the American declaration of independence. Rousseau supplies a standard of self-legislation against which even democracies can be judged, since a majority that legislates for particular persons and not for citizens as equals departs from the general will. Even Hobbes contributes a standard: order is the first duty of government, and where anarchy actually prevails his argument for absolutism regains its force. The distinction that resolves the question is between explanation and justification — the theories were never good accounts of prehistory and were always intended as accounts of legitimacy — and a strong answer shows that their historical failure does not entail their normative failure, while noting that a standard detached from any account of how people actually live can become an abstraction that proves too much.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the explanation/justification distinction to be argued with specific evidence from at least two thinkers and a judgement on how far legitimacy can be established without historical consent.
